title: Maharani Jind Kaur
hookLine: his youngest queen, mother of Duleep Singh, would later defy an empire

cards: A woman's name keeps turning up in the letters of British officials, and not kindly. They write of her as difficult, even dangerous. They try to keep her away from her son, and move her from place to place.
Years after the Maharaja is gone, she's still someone they worry about in the Punjab. Who was she? She began as the youngest of the Maharaja's queens.

teach.b: Sikh histories say Jind Kaur was the daughter of a man who looked after the royal kennels, not a princess from a great house.
She married the Maharaja late in his life, the youngest of his queens, and gave birth to Duleep Singh, his youngest son.
When the Maharaja died, the boy was still a baby, with older brothers and powerful ministers between him and the throne.

teach.h: A QUEEN WHO WOULD STAND UP.
teach.b: Few would have guessed he'd ever sit on it. Without spoiling the story ahead: the throne of Lahore would pass through several hands, fast and violently, and in time it reached her son.
Then Jind Kaur stood up as regent and spoke for him, in a court full of men, with a foreign empire at the border. She would be separated from him and imprisoned, and still she wouldn't give in.
That's what it means to say she defied an empire, and you'll walk through it day by day.
Look back at this week: Peshawar at the edge, the mountain of light, a court of many faiths, a ruler remembered for mercy, gifts to the Tenth Guru's places, the court in paint.

teach.h: A WEEK OF A KINGDOM AT ITS HEIGHT.
teach.b: A kingdom at its height, and standing quietly in it, a young queen whose courage hadn't yet been tested.
The Gurus taught that a woman is not less: Guru Nanak asked why anyone would call her lowly, from whom kings are born. Jind Kaur would answer that question in her own way.

how: Sikhs remember Maharani Jind Kaur in histories of the end of the Sikh kingdom, and honor her as a mother and queen who would not give in.

games.q: you're the youngest queen. after many changes, the throne reaches your small son, in a court full of men, with a foreign empire at the border. what do you do?
o: stay in the background and let the ministers decide.
stand up as regent and speak for your son.
games.why: Jind Kaur stood up as regent and spoke for Duleep Singh, and later, separated from him and imprisoned, she still wouldn't give in.

practice: Bring to mind a mother who was brave: your own, a grandmother, a friend raising children alone, or one you've only read about.
Picture her face and one hard thing she faced and didn't run from, and hold her in your mind with honor, breath by breath. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Jind Kaur, the youngest of the Maharaja's queens, mother of Duleep Singh, who would one day stand up to an empire for her son.

orig.note: Jind Kaur; Kaur is the name Sikh women carry.
